Forecast Discussion

A front moved through the region last night, which will stand to direct more of the afternoon shower activity a bit further south in the mountains. However, we still expect scattered showers and some thunder up this way.

Transient, weak high pressure well off to the northeast provides a bit of a wedge Saturday, which allows for cooler conditions than the record highs a couple of days ago. Temperatures don’t change too much even as the high pulls away, likely a touch warmer Sunday and Monday. Both of those days will continue a stretch of scattered showers & thunderstorms.

Tuesday is noticeably cooler than the next few days with continued showers & thunder. A much stronger high pressure system begins to build in from the northeast, which will mark the transition to our first period of a fall feel.

Even cooler conditions settle in Wednesday as the wedge takes full effect. Cloudy skies and showers deliver below normal temperatures that some may find worthy of long sleeves. Thursday will feature less shower activity, but will continue to be cool and cloudy. We’ll start to slip out of the wedge next Friday (albeit with continued showers) as drier air may try to work in for next weekend.

Sep 14, 2026
Sizzling Start to September
A Hot Summer Send-Off

School is back in session, football season has kicked off, and young parking lot maple trees are showing their colors first, as they always do. You would never know it was September if you had awoken from a coma on Wednesday of last week (Sep. 2nd) and walked outside. Many stations across the Southern Appalachian region reached new daily record high temperatures, with all stations posting highs that would be considered "above average" any day of the year, let alone early September. While it is true the start of September is not a traditionally cool time, and Labor Day weekend is quite the busy stretch on beaches and lakes, this heat was anomalous.

Nothing Like Last Year

The first week of September 2025 was a delight to hot-weather haters! High temperatures were in the vicinity of 15 to 20 degrees cooler than 2026's, with low temperatures dipping into the 40s in Boone on 9/1 and 9/2, 2025. The chart below displays the high and low temperatures (both observed and average) at the Watauga County Hospital station in Boone for September 2025.

Now, let's look at the same plot for September 2026, thus far. Notice how high above the faint red average high temperature line Boone got, especially compared to 2025!

It wasn't just the High Country that felt fall-like relief last year, either. Hickory had just 3 high temperatures above 80 degrees in the first 7 days of Sept. 2025, whereas this year 6 of 7 were above 80, and 5 of 7 above 90. These numbers aren't remarkably well below normal, but the stark contrast with the deep-frying we experienced last week makes the heat that much harder to stomach.

For further comparison, Asheville experienced an average temperature of 68.6F in the first 7 days of Sept. 2025. That was cooler than average by 2.8 degrees, but was only the 28th-coldest first week of September on record there. Meanwhile in 2026, the first 7 days posted an average temperature of 77.1F, nearly 9 degrees warmer than last year, and 5.7 degrees above average. Not to mention, it was the warmest first week of September in the 81 year history of the Asheville Airport weather station. The same can be said for several sites around our area, including Hickory, where the average temperature was at 80.7F for the week. That is most similar to Jacksonville, Florida's climate for early September, and is above average for any 7-day period in Hickory, including mid-July.

Crunching Numbers

The map above displays where the high temperature for September 3rd, 2026 wound up in the all-time ranking of high temperatures for that date at each site. The 1s indicate that that station experienced its warmest Sept. 3rd high temperature on record, 2s indicate 2nd warmest... and so on. As you can see, there are plenty of 1s, 2s, and 3s.

In Boone, high temperatures at the station at the water treatment facility east of downtown reached 84F, 85F, and 86F from the 2nd to the 4th. At our station on top of the office building on Blowing Rock Road, highs reached 89F, 88F, and 89F on the same days. The extra concrete does wonders for high temperatures on the hottest days. Prior to this past week, Boone had not experienced 4 consecutive highs of 85F or greater since 1954. Only 5 total days in every September since 1980 made it to 85F, and in the entire period of record (1929-2025), only 39 total days achieved this. That is just 1.3% of September days in Boone reaching 85 degrees in the last 90+ years. That is a whole bunch of numbers to make the point... it was really, really hot.

In Wytheville, highs reached into the 90s 4 consecutive days (Sept. 1-4), but fell just shy of records each day. Those were the first September days above 90 degrees since 2019, raising the total since 2010 to just fifteen September 90s.

Summertime Totals

The total number of 90 degree days in a year can be a decent measurement for how hot that summer was. There are some details lost in such a simple statistic, but it works as a basic guide. Hickory has logged 37 days at or above 90 degrees in 2026 thus far, which is 6 more days than average (31.2 days). In September, Hickory average just 2.73 days at or above 90F, with the most being 13 in 1954. There have been 5 so far in Sept. 2026.

The map below shows the number of 90 degree days for the Southern Appalachians thus far in 2026, through Labor Day. Obviously, the terrain is the main factor in determining who gets 90 and who doesn't.

Here is the same map, but zoomed out to show the heat of the North Carolina coastal plain. It is remarkable the variance in climate that one can experience within less than a half day's drive.

The worst of the heat has passed, and now we look forward for a real fall feel. Lenoir has yet to dip below 50 degrees this fall. On average, Lenoir's first low temperature in the 40s falls on September 2nd, with the latest wait for 40s pushing into mid-October. There is not any real sign of 2026's wait ending soon, but before you know it, the leaves will change and the winds will blow strong from the northwest once more.
